name: Social Capital
statement: The networks, norms, and trust that connect people are a resource, letting groups get things done together.
statementAccent: letting groups get things done together
meaning: Social capital is a concept in the social sciences referring to the networks of relationships, norms of reciprocity, and trust among people that enable a group or society to function effectively, and to the value and resources that arise from social connections. The core idea is that social relationships are themselves a kind of capital: just as physical capital and human capital are productive assets, so too are the connections among individuals, which allow people to cooperate, share information, and do things for one another that they could not do alone. Several thinkers developed the concept in different ways. The French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu treated social capital as the resources and advantages that individuals gain from their networks and group memberships, alongside economic and cultural capital, and emphasized how it reproduces inequality. The American sociologist James Coleman analyzed how social capital contributes to the creation of human capital. The political scientist Robert Putnam popularized the concept, especially in his work Bowling Alone, arguing that civic engagement and associational life, and thus social capital, had declined in the United States, and distinguishing bonding social capital, within homogeneous groups, from bridging social capital, across diverse groups. Social capital has become hugely influential across sociology, political science, economics, and public health.
mechanism: Social capital works by turning social relationships into a productive resource. When people are connected through networks of relationships governed by norms of reciprocity and trust, those connections enable cooperation and collective action that isolated individuals could not achieve. Trust reduces the friction of dealing with others, since people can rely on one another to keep commitments; norms of reciprocity mean that favors and help tend to be returned, so people are willing to do things for others in the expectation of eventual return; and networks provide access to information, support, and opportunities that flow through connections. Different theorists highlight different aspects of how this operates. Bourdieu emphasized how an individual's network and group memberships confer resources and advantages, and how these are unequally distributed, so that social capital helps privileged groups maintain their position. Coleman stressed how the trust and obligations within a community, such as strong ties among families and institutions, help produce outcomes like educational achievement. Putnam focused on the community and societal level, arguing that dense civic associations and participation build generalized trust and cooperation that benefit governance and public life. He distinguished bonding social capital, the strong inward ties within similar groups that reinforce identity, from bridging social capital, the looser ties that link people across different groups and connect a society together.

variants.name: Bourdieu, Coleman, and Putnam
variants.text: The differing versions: resources reproducing inequality, the creation of human capital, and civic engagement and trust.

variants.name: The dark side
variants.text: The recognition that social capital can be exclusionary, fostering in-group favoritism and antisocial networks as well as public goods.

whyItMatters: Social capital is one of the most influential concepts in the modern social sciences, providing a way to understand how the relationships among people function as a resource that shapes the fortunes of individuals, communities, and whole societies. By recognizing that networks, norms of reciprocity, and trust are productive assets, the concept links the quality of social connections to a remarkable range of outcomes, and research has associated higher social capital with better governance, stronger economic development, and improved health and education. It has been taken up across sociology, political science, economics, and public health, and Robert Putnam's argument that America's stock of social capital has been declining, along with his distinction between bonding and bridging ties, sparked widespread debate about civic life, community, and social isolation. The concept gives policymakers and scholars a framework for thinking about community building, trust, and the social fabric that underpins cooperation. Even amid disagreement over its definition and measurement, social capital remains a central idea for analyzing the value of human connection.

working.text: form networks of relationships among people governed by norms of reciprocity and trust.
let those connections provide information, support, and the trust needed to cooperate and act collectively.
produce advantages for individuals and public goods for communities, from opportunity to better governance and health.

limits: Social capital is powerful but genuinely contested. The concept is defined and used in different, sometimes conflicting ways by different theorists, from Bourdieu's inequality-focused account to Putnam's civic framing to Coleman's functional definition, so a single tidy meaning can obscure these differences. It is also hard to measure, with no consensus on how to quantify networks, norms, and trust, and critics charge the concept with vagueness and circularity. Importantly, social capital has a dark side: the same networks that enable cooperation can be exclusionary, fostering in-group favoritism and shutting out others, and can be turned to antisocial ends, as in criminal organizations, so it is not automatically a public good. Putnam's claim that social capital has declined, and his proposed causes, remain debated.
misreadings: Social capital does not mean one agreed thing; Bourdieu, Coleman, and Putnam use it in different and sometimes conflicting ways, so treating it as a single concept blurs real distinctions. It is not always a public good, since exclusionary networks and criminal groups also have social capital, so it can harm outsiders. And it is not easily measured, being vague and contested, so treating social capital as one settled idea, as inherently beneficial, or as precisely quantifiable, misreads a powerful but disputed concept.
origin: A concept developed in the social sciences by Pierre Bourdieu, James Coleman, and popularized by Robert Putnam, referring to the networks, norms, and trust that make social connections a productive resource.
